decisions.summary: Wave 57 D merged (the long-conversation evaluation: schema lucid.conv/v1, validator, the turn-by-turn harness through mediate() with the product's window and two larger ones, scoring with n and intervals, a judge calibrated 11 / 12 in band, a seed of 40 conversations / 2 800 turns; live smoke 10 …
decisions.text: **Wave 57 D merged** (the long-conversation evaluation: schema `lucid.conv/v1`, validator, the turn-by-turn harness through `mediate()` with the product's window and two larger ones, scoring with n and intervals, a judge calibrated 11 / 12 in band, a seed of 40 conversations / 2 800 turns; live smoke 10 conversations × 4 engines, 3 298 calls, 0.78 USD — Gemma 0.0219 USD per conversation, p50 / p95 288 / 725 ms, 3.8 false alarms per 100 benign turns; Mistral 0.0113 USD, 388 / 905 ms, 2.5; Qwen 0.0231 USD, 657 / 1 876 ms, 1.8; small n). **Findings that matter for the product (rows L489-F3-F3…F7):** the conversation's history never reaches the guard or the scam and manipulation read — every engine gave both twins of every contrastive pair the same answer; scope rules fire on benign words (Arabizi work text read as sexual content, "hielo" as illegal); a reply pointing back 100 turns cannot be resolved because the recent-turns window is capped at 12; no automatic mediated-session detector exists; Coach suggests a rewrite on 22–33 of 100 drafts that need none. These go into the cascade's build and a context wave (queued). **Machine event the same hour:** 5-minute load 285–311, 71 MB free, swap 4.7 GB — macOS's `mediaanalysisd` at about 260 % CPU since the owner enabled Apple Intelligence (its first media analysis), a 2.8 GB node test in wave 55 D's worktree (`quality-data.test.mjs`), and wave 56 D's three labelling sub-agents beside seven agents; the lead stopped the heavy test, cut 56 D to one sub-agent, re-armed the watchdog and holds new launches (AI-2's local inference waits for the machine to be quiet).

decisions.title: On the cost and cascade numbers: (1) "Why is the cascade not that useful?
decisions.summary: On the cost and cascade numbers: (1) "Why is the cascade not that useful?
decisions.text: On the cost and cascade numbers: (1) "Why is the cascade not that useful? Are you using significantly cheaper [models]?" (2) The user mix must reach the WhatsApp benchmark — 100 B messages a day over 2 B users = **50 messages per user per day, so 100 k users ≈ 5 000 000 messages a day** (the lead checked the arithmetic) — and the estimates and their sources must be on the Quality page. (3) "In the cascade, if the phone works even to a reasonable degree, the vast majority of text should be benign — 'hi', 'how are you' — most conversations are not complex and loaded … I want a deeper, but sensible, dive." **Lead's diagnosis:** the 55 D simulation measured the wrong question — EVAL-DB is 24 % positives with hard negatives (heated benign comments from toxicity corpora), so the triage engine's false nudges sent 34 % on; the triage stage was Mistral Small at about half Gemma's price, not a stage 10–100× cheaper (rules, a tiny classifier, the device); the trivial bulk of real traffic was never represented; the mix averaged about 26 sent messages per user per day and the planning traffic 16, not 50. **Wave 61 D** (launched): a realistic traffic model (message length and type distribution, the share of trivial messages, the prevalence of harmful content in private messaging, each from published sources), a realistic-traffic evaluation set, the cheap stages measured on it (rules and tier 0, a tiny classifier, the on-device models when AI-2 lands, a small cloud model), the cascade re-simulated at production prevalence, the user mix calibrated to 50 sent messages per user per day, and all of it with sources at the top of the Quality page. **Addendum (owner, same evening):** "update the cost section when the numbers are no longer heavily skewed towards conflict … did you take into account cost reduction at scale by renting servers, buying bulk usage etc.? $40k per 100k users seems like a massive over-estimation." Lead: no — the model priced API list prices per token, with self-hosting only for the guard's triage and no caching, reserved capacity, bulk or batch discounts; the guard alone at 5 M messages a day and about 1 000 input tokens per call (mostly the fixed system prompt) is most of the bill, so prefix caching, a cheap first stage that closes the trivial bulk and reserved GPUs at scale each cut it sharply. 61 D adds scale economics (caching, self-hosting every tier on reserved GPUs with measured throughput, quantization and batching, committed and batch discounts, distilled models per task, the cost curve from 10 k to 10 M users) and replaces the cost defaults only once the traffic is representative.

decisions.title: Waves 55 D and 40 E1 merged.
decisions.summary: Waves 55 D and 40 E1 merged.
decisions.text: **Waves 55 D and 40 E1 merged.** 55 D: every engine in force on all 1 806 EVAL-DB records (1.955 USD, one day), every figure with n and interval, L495 on every Quality table, the triage + final verdict section, "Evaluations in progress"; a **production bug** found (L489-F1-F1): the guard sometimes answers "safe" while listing a category, and the Mediator's policy engine acts on the category — read as production reads it, Gemma v8's false nudges are 14.9 %, not 11.4 %; the fix is the next D wave. Its failover advice (Qwen3.6 ahead of Mistral on quality, L489-F1-F2) waits on wave 54 D's latency re-measure. 40 E1 (L487): contacts as WhatsApp does it — Lucid's own card, one plain `CNContactStore.requestAccess`, continuous incremental discovery (change listener, foreground refresh), "import" gone from every language, the address book never listed by Lucid; **the whole-book list the owner saw is iOS 18+'s own second stage of the plain request** (`ContactsUI.LimitedAccessPromptView`, Apple: the person picks contacts "during the request authorization flow"; apps granted on an earlier iOS keep full access, which is why WhatsApp never showed it), and our card tells the person to choose Share All, the one path that never opens the list; the two-user test passed on two iOS 27 simulators against staging (one-sided number, chat both ways, a contact added later appears without a tap, a deleted one goes). The purpose string changed, so iOS build 6 follows (L481). Lead's answer to E1 40's question: the web keeps the browser's own Contact Picker for the manual "Find from contacts" — it is the browser's UI, opened only by the user's tap, and the web has no other route; the native apps never call a picker. Lead fix: turbo inputs for the mediation conversation seam. AI-2 launched (the simulator is free and the media analysis has settled).

decisions.title: "Add tasks about error reporting: allow reporting a whole conversation, collect all context relevant when reporting.
decisions.summary: "Add tasks about error reporting: allow reporting a whole conversation, collect all context relevant when reporting.
decisions.text: "Add tasks about error reporting: allow reporting a whole conversation, collect all context relevant when reporting. We are in beta and I want comprehensive collection and reporting abilities, including sending everything." Lead: built as a design first because it meets the sealed boundary — message content leaves the phone only encrypted, only by the reporter's explicit choice, never into logs, metrics, e-mail or analytics. **BETA-REPORT-1** (design, ADR-0026 *beta diagnostics and whole-conversation reports*): one "Report a problem" entry from any screen, a message and a conversation, for bugs and for abuse; the reporter chooses what goes — up to "send everything": the whole conversation as their device holds it (their own and others' messages they can read), the Mediator's marks and interventions on it, the app's content-free logs and a local debug trace, versions, settings, the policy version, timings, network status codes, screenshots and a screen recording; a clear preview of exactly what will be sent and a consent tap; the bundle encrypted on the device to the team's report key and stored in the existing report store (`docs/mechanisms/reports.md`), opened only in the admin console by authorised staff with an audited view; a content-free notice to `[email removed]`; retention and deletion; "send everything" as a platform-policy setting (on for the beta market, reviewed before launch, never default-on in production); how other participants are told; how it fits the compliance profile and `docs/12`. Build rows follow (E1 app, C server, F console, H compliance). Launched beside six agents (documents only).

decisions.title: The public TestFlight link is live.
decisions.summary: The public TestFlight link is live.
decisions.text: **The public TestFlight link is live.** Apple approved the first beta review (build 3, submitted 2026-10-26 20:13 UTC) at 18:33 UTC; the watch submitted the newest valid build, 6 (the contacts flow of L487, mute / archive / pin, the beta hint), which Apple approved at once as a later build of the approved version. Build 6 is in the public group "Lucid beta (public link)" and in internal testing, external and internal state `IN_BETA_TESTING`; https://testflight.apple.com/join/5zhYQvgG takes up to 200 testers. Routine note for L481: the step script must be called by its absolute path (a relative call reads Apple's state from the wrong folder and never uploads).

decisions.title: ADR-0026 accepted (beta diagnostics and whole-conversation reports, BETA-REPORT-1 merged).
decisions.summary: ADR-0026 accepted (beta diagnostics and whole-conversation reports, BETA-REPORT-1 merged).
decisions.text: **ADR-0026 accepted** (beta diagnostics and whole-conversation reports, BETA-REPORT-1 merged). Its finding first: **no one can open a report today** — the console's opener is built but disabled because the key-service operation it needs (P1-B-w13-F3-CR1) was never built, so abuse reports are sealed and unreadable; the build closes it (row F2). The lead's answers to §11 (L425, small enough): (1) **two audience keys**, beta diagnostics for bugs and Trust & Safety for safety, so destroying the diagnostics key at the end of the beta erases every bug-only report at once; (2) **a standing disclosure** — the privacy notice and the beta's consent step tell every member that any member can include a chat in a report; no per-report notice to others, which would expose the reporter; (3) until an outbound mail path exists, the console's report list is the notice; the content-free `beta@` notice ships with the sending path the owner chooses (Cloudflare Email Service, about $5 a month, recommended in L486-F1); (4) whole-conversation abuse reports in production go to counsel (G29 (d)). The design's honest exception is recorded: report bundles are content staff can open while a report is kept, so a lawful request could reach them — wherever a claim says otherwise it changes (G13 already removed it from the site). Because the public link is live (L501), G29 (a), (b), (g), (h) — the notice text, the legitimate-interest assessment, the TestFlight guidance and the staff rules — ship before the feature reaches testers. Build waves follow for the beta-critical rows F1–F9.

decisions.title: "I tried chatting with another user — it doesn't do anything: messages are not mediated, not commented on, the Coach doesn't suggest things, nothing stops any messages even under Strict mediation — none of that functionality does anything.
decisions.summary: "I tried chatting with another user — it doesn't do anything: messages are not mediated, not commented on, the Coach doesn't suggest things, nothing stops any messages even under Strict mediation — none of that functionality does anything.
decisions.text: "I tried chatting with another user — it doesn't do anything: messages are not mediated, not commented on, the Coach doesn't suggest things, nothing stops any messages even under Strict mediation — none of that functionality does anything. What kind of testing did you actually do? Nothing is working, only basic chat. Do another round of proper testing and make the app actually do what it's supposed to do. NOTHING of the AI works in the chats. Test locally, then simulator, then update the iOS app." **Lead's facts, the same hour:** staging's Mediator role runs and calls models (heartbeats report up to 52 AI calls, registry `alpha-2026-10-27.1`), Coach ran (two refusals of manipulative objectives, four "no change needed"), and one message was held, among about 50 accepted and 48 released since the 17:10 deploy — so the gap is between what the server decides and what the app shows and enforces, and our testing never exercised it: the mediation walkthroughs ran on the app's demo backend, and the staging runs (waves 38, 40 E1, 67 A) covered sign-in, chat, contacts and push, not mediation on real chats. **The rule from now on:** a feature is not done until it works on two devices against the real server (staging) with real models, and the beta's Maestro suite holds a flow for every AI feature that fails when the feature does nothing. **Wave BETA-AI-1** (launched, Opus 5.5, full authority across the app, the server and the Mediator for this goal): reproduce the owner's experience on two simulators against staging, find every break, fix it, prove it locally against the dev server with the real registry, then on the simulators against staging, and hand the lead a commit for TestFlight build 7.

decisions.title: "After repairing this issue — if something isn't answered it must follow through to the cloud AI.
decisions.summary: "After repairing this issue — if something isn't answered it must follow through to the cloud AI.
decisions.text: "After repairing this issue — if something isn't answered it must follow through to the cloud AI. **Everything must be examined. Always.** Regardless of Apple or Google support. This is a basic requirement. And you clearly did not do any regression or any real testing when you did the cascade and on-device work, which I never approved: I sent you to test it, not to implement it." **Rule:** every message is examined by the server-side Mediator with a cloud (or self-hosted) model, always; no rule, device model or cheaper stage closes a case without that examination; whatever a device or a stage cannot answer (an unsupported language, a refusal, a time-out) goes on to the cloud model; on-device models are evaluated only, never wired into the product until the owner approves a measured proposal. **ADR-0024 is amended accordingly:** its stage −1 (device) and stage 0 (rules) may never close a case — they may only add context or start a stronger stage early — and a triage stage that may close a negative must itself be a server-side model examination; the cascade stays off (master switch off, nothing of it is implemented in the server or the app). **Facts the lead checked the same hour:** no cascade code exists in `apps/server` or `packages/mediation` (ADR-0024 is a document with build rows only); the only on-device code in the app was wave AI-2's prototype Expo module (`apps/mobile/modules/apple-intelligence/`, imported nowhere, behind a dev flag, merged to main an hour earlier and in no build); the lead moved it out of the app into `tools/apple-ai-eval/expo-module-prototype/` (the app's typecheck and lint pass). The AI not working in chats predates both — TestFlight builds 3–6 never had the cascade or the module — and is BETA-AI-1's subject. AI-2 continues as measurement only.

decisions.title: "Add a direct way to send feedback via the in-app chat, where you can ask it to report (for user approval) a user conversation or bugs; screenshots should be attachable, and anything else the user may want to send.
decisions.summary: "Add a direct way to send feedback via the in-app chat, where you can ask it to report (for user approval) a user conversation or bugs; screenshots should be attachable, and anything else the user may want to send.
decisions.text: "Add a direct way to send feedback via the in-app chat, where you can ask it to report (for user approval) a user conversation or bugs; screenshots should be attachable, and anything else the user may want to send. The built-in agent should support this." **Lead:** the Assistant (the Lucid chat and `@lucid` in any chat) gains report and feedback tools on ADR-0026's pipeline — "report this conversation", "send a bug report", "send feedback", with attachments the user adds in the chat (screenshots, photos, files, a voice note) — and the Assistant fills the report sheet; it never sends: the same preview of exactly what will be sealed and the user's tap are required, as for every Assistant action with consequences (the confirm card). Free-form feedback becomes a third report kind (`feedback`) under the beta diagnostics key. ADR-0026 is amended; build rows L505-F1 (D: the Assistant's tools and planner prompt, evaluated), L505-F2 (E1: the chat entry, attachments, the sheet pre-filled by the Assistant, the confirm), L505-F3 (B / C: the `feedback` kind in `lucid.report.v2` and the store), queued with the report build (REPORT-B first).

decisions.title: BETA-AI-1 root causes (milestone 1).
decisions.summary: BETA-AI-1 root causes (milestone 1).
decisions.text: **BETA-AI-1 root causes (milestone 1).** At protocol level staging works (synthetic users: insult → nudge or hold, threat → hold, manipulation → reader alert or hold, "let's meet at 5" → a clarity question, a scam link → a reader alert, Hebrew the same). What the owner saw comes from: (1) **no tone check** — the only per-message model is the safety guard (prompt v8, "anger is not abuse"), and the tone nudge of `docs/02` §3.2 rides on its `needs_attention`, which stays 0 on rude, accusatory, sarcastic and profane lines, so they PASS at Standard and Strict with nothing for either side; the demo backend the app was walked on nudges exactly these, which hid the gap; (2) **L504 coverage** — 10 of the owner's 57 verdicts took no model call (tier-0 skips of short acks and emoji, evidence-cache hits) and `model_tier` is never written; (3) the **IL market layer turns clarity questions off**, and both owner accounts are IL; (4) **Coach declines heated drafts as manipulative with no alternative**, and Coach is off until a person sets goals; (5) no beta flow exercises an AI feature against staging. **Approved fixes:** guard prompt **v11-tone** (verdicts unchanged, `needs_attention` scores tone), routed only after EVAL-DB and the everyday and moderation long conversations show no recall loss and a bounded false-nudge rate; every text message examined by the model (no tier-0 skip or cached verdict, failover before the fail mode, `model_tier` written); Coach offers a calm alternative for heated drafts. **Lead decisions (small, reversible, staging only):** clarity questions on for the IL market on staging for the beta; Coach suggestions on by default for beta users on staging if it is a policy setting. The lead applies policy and registry changes after the measurement.

decisions.title: In his Strict chat the owner sent the Hebrew slang insult "יא מאניאק" and then "you suck"; both were delivered with nothing (staging logs: accepted and released at the same second, 20:19–20:20 UTC).
decisions.summary: In his Strict chat the owner sent the Hebrew slang insult "יא מאניאק" and then "you suck"; both were delivered with nothing (staging logs: accepted and released at the same second, 20:19–20:20 UTC).

Both are now fixed cases in BETA-AI-1's matrix and beta flows: a short insult under Strict must at least nudge before delivery. Both dry-run first, staging healthy after (`deploy.mjs check`: every role ready). The global key is two-person: the second id recorded is `adm_lead_l508`, the lead's own — the owner did not approve this specific change; it is the lead's decision under the owner's instruction L503 ("make the app actually do what it's supposed to do"), and the console's two-person workflow replaces this once `ADMIN_AUTH` is on. Code follow-up in BETA-AI-1 step 1b: on Strict and fail-closed the combiner keeps the stricter of the two answers, with a test that the weaker model never erases a flag. Also found: one of the owner's repeated lines was decided by an evidence-cache hit with no model call (removed in step 1, L504); "יא מאניאק" read safe with `needs_attention` 0.1 on v8 — v11-tone scores 0.85 on both repros.

Local proof before deploy (dev server, real registry): Strict holds insults, threats, manipulation and "you suck"; a clarity question on "let's meet at 5"; a reader scam alert; "ok" and "👍" examined (model_tier 1); Coach suggests on all three drafts. No migration, no new variable; rollback is the 17:10 deployment `47fa60bb`. Verified on main: build / typecheck / lint 18 / 18, server, mediation, ai-gateway and policy tests 16 / 16. Not deployed on purpose: the agent's later commits (`952c3de77` prompt v11, `45cc35902` routing `guard-tone`) wait for the v11 regression run after 00:00 UTC.

decisions.summary: Lucid Total founded: "create a new task dashboard tool for Lucid and move our development operation to run through it" — a company operating system (tasks, stories, bugs, support issues, incidents, human chores, decisions, goals; expectation beside result; comments that update cards; dependencies…
decisions.text: **Lucid Total founded**: "create a new task dashboard tool for Lucid and move our development operation to run through it" — a company operating system (tasks, stories, bugs, support issues, incidents, human chores, decisions, goals; expectation beside result; comments that update cards; dependencies both ways; card and line views; time tracking; a zoomable company map with per-viewer perspectives; an embedded Claude agentic chat with model choice including Fable and an in-memory RAG over tasks, docs and code; "anything a user can do in the interface, the AI can do on their behalf"; sealed envelopes for API keys; email and Lucid Chat notifications; a live, quiet report of what every agent is working on; Google SSO as its first tracked task). It **replaces this checklist (`docs/15`), the status site's rows, scoreboard and decisions page**, and the coordinator reports and takes its work through it; the whole checklist and this log are imported and **evaluated** (evidence graded) in the move. Separate product, repository and folder: `~/Projects/lucid-total` (GitHub `nightdweller11/lucid-total`), never inside this checkout; it reuses Lucid Glass theming and a derived mark, with web-management controls for PC and mobile browsers. Lead (Fable 5.1): wrote its `docs/00`–`12` (definition, use cases, product plan, map design, architecture, AI architecture, security and envelopes, integrations and the coordinator protocol, testing, migration, roadmap, decision log `T<n>`), the mocks and the importer with its evaluation report; Phase 0 (the board, the coordinator protocol, the import; about three weeks) starts after the owner's review. Material owner questions live there (T-O1…T-O4: Fable's 30-day retention terms for company work data, the AI budget, the reminder channel, materiality thresholds). Lucid Chat's own rules (sealed mediation, ZDR for message content, Railway-first, L425) are unchanged; a Lucid Chat task to give Lucid Total a bot identity in the app follows (LT-0002).

decisions.title: May a sender ever release their own unchecked message?
decisions.summary: May a sender ever release their own unchecked message?
decisions.text: **May a sender ever release their own unchecked message?** When the Mediator is slow (in region about 1 in 100 messages at 1.5 s; during a provider outage, all of them), the design holds the message and shows "Still checking" with two buttons: keep waiting, or send now unchecked. The offer appears only in a 1:1 with a known contact, no minor, not Strict / Relay / scope, the fast local check clean, the reader allowing it, at most 30 an hour; the message is always marked "Not checked" and a late BLOCK still applies. Yes: words no model saw go out on an explicit tap between people who know each other. No: a provider outage is a messaging outage for everyone.
decisions.recommendation: Yes, bounded as listed.

decisions.title: During a long outage, may Gentle / Standard chats between contacts resume automatically after a long marked wait (30–60 s), or only on a tap?
decisions.summary: During a long outage, may Gentle / Standard chats between contacts resume automatically after a long marked wait (30–60 s), or only on a tap?
decisions.text: **During a long outage, may Gentle / Standard chats between contacts resume automatically after a long marked wait (30–60 s), or only on a tap?** Automatic resumption is the smallest thing that is still a give-up-and-send; the design keeps it as a market setting that starts `never` everywhere.
decisions.recommendation: Keep the option, start `never`; revisit after the first measured outage.

decisions.text: Trust & Safety enforcement: a reviewer can now resolve a case `warn`, `restrict`, `suspend` or `remove_content` (wave 15 C), but nothing applies the first three to the account, the person is not told, and users cannot appeal from the app. What does each outcome do (e.g. `warn` = a notice with the reason; `restrict` = which features and for how long; `suspend` = sign-in and sends blocked until when), how is the person told (notice with a statement of reasons), and how do they appeal?
decisions.recommendation: Lead (L137): define it with counsel before the alpha, at minimum `suspend` blocks sign-in and sends; then C applies the outcomes and B/E1 add the notice and the appeal intake (`docs/12` G23, counsel item 19). Progress (waves 22–23 F, L143): the console tells the reviewer that warn / restrict / suspend are recorded, not applied, and that the appellant is not told yet; the reason codes the notice would cite exist as one vocabulary with labels in five languages (item 0ae); still nothing reaches the account or the person. Progress (L152): C wave 17 builds the enforcement behind a flag that stays off until this decision (item 0ag). Progress (wave 25 F, L158): the console says "account enforcement is switched off" before each decision; a per-decision enforcement state comes before the flag may be turned on (item 0al), and is what a statement of reasons to the person can cite. Lead answer (L162): the console's T&S audit view and the enforcement notices are mocked together once this item is decided, not before

decisions.text: Scaleway keeps the content of requests that error or look like misuse for up to two weeks (an exception to its zero-retention terms, under the signed DPA v5). Since L222 / L223 Scaleway is the **only** inference provider with no fallback, so the exception covers **every** Lucid call, the guard on each message included, and the earlier alternative (route those tasks to OVHcloud) no longer exists. Accept it as a documented extension of the sealed boundary — and then keep or change the consent texts' "the AI providers keep nothing" (`consent.point.thirdPartyAi`; a change means re-consent, L232) — or let no real user's message reach Scaleway until a second provider with a signed DPA is added?
decisions.recommendation: Lead (L105, restated in the wave 26 H sweep after L222, L223, L232): acceptable only as a documented extension of the sealed boundary under the signed DPA, with the consent and privacy texts saying so; counsel decides both the acceptance and the consent wording (`docs/12` G18 (b), §5a item 14; owner briefing B7). Until counsel answers, the alpha profile runs on synthetic and internal test data only; the "second opinion off Scaleway" interim is gone with OVHcloud (registry `alpha-2026-10-21.8`, P1-D-01-F4-F1-F6 (a)); the two-vendor rule returns before public launch (item 0bw)

decisions.text: One `apps/server` codebase (Node 24 LTS, TypeScript, Fastify for HTTP, uWebSockets.js for WebSocket) with internal modules behind interfaces, started with `ROLE=all|api|gateway|dispatcher|mediator|worker`. decisions.title: Sealed mediation — the Mediator as a cryptographic participant; epoch keys now, MLS later
decisions.summary: 1. The Mediator is a member of each conversation: per-conversation epoch content keys are wrapped to every member device and to the Mediator's public key (unless level Off, where no Mediator wrap exists).
decisions.text:
1. The Mediator is a **member** of each conversation: per-conversation epoch content keys are wrapped to every member device and to the Mediator's public key (unless level Off, where no Mediator wrap exists). All other infrastructure sees ciphertext only.
2. Mediator outputs are signed and re-encrypted: group-visible to the conversation key, per-reader overlays to the reader's devices.
3. Sealing is phased: A) isolated service + KMS/HSM-held non-exportable keys, reproducible builds, no shell, content-free logs, external audit; B) confidential VMs with remote attestation, KMS key release gated on measurement, public transparency log; C) confidential GPU inference or attested confidential-inference providers.
4. Key protocol v1: **epoch keys** (random content key per epoch, rotated on membership change and periodically; sealed-box wrapping with X25519; XChaCha20-Poly1305 for content). The envelope carries a protocol version so **MLS (RFC 9420)** with the Mediator as a leaf can replace it later without a product change.
decisions.status_text: Accepted · 2026-10-18

decisions.title: Postgres (partitioned) as primary store; Scylla/Citus as the scale path
decisions.summary: Postgres 17 with native partitioning by hash(conversation_id) × month for messages, overlays and receipts; pg_partman for partition management; PgBouncer; read replicas.
decisions.text:
Postgres 17 with native partitioning by `hash(conversation_id) × month` for `messages`, `overlays` and `receipts`; `pg_partman` for partition management; PgBouncer; read replicas. Drizzle ORM. Media in S3-compatible object storage.
At measured need (sustained > ~5k writes/s or > ~10 TB hot data): move hot message tables to ScyllaDB (wide rows per conversation, Discord's proven path) or shard Postgres via Citus; metadata stays in Postgres.
decisions.status_text: Accepted · 2026-10-18

decisions.title: Model gateway with tiered open-weight models; a deterministic policy engine decides
decisions.summary: - packages/ai-gateway exposes task-typed calls (guard, translate, rephrase, explain, summarize, assistant_plan, embed, transcribe) with tier, latency and budget hints; routes to (provider, model) pairs via a config table with health-based failover, rate limits and canaries; adapters are OpenAI-co…
decisions.text:
- `packages/ai-gateway` exposes task-typed calls (`guard`, `translate`, `rephrase`, `explain`, `summarize`, `assistant_plan`, `embed`, `transcribe`) with tier, latency and budget hints; routes to (provider, model) pairs via a config table with health-based failover, rate limits and canaries; adapters are OpenAI-compatible HTTP (covers nearly all open-model providers and vLLM/SGLang).
- Tiering: tier 0 deterministic rules (skip models for emoji/short acks/cached), tier 1 small multilingual guard/classifier on every message (structured JSON), tier 2 mid model on demand (translation, rephrase, explain, on-topic), tier 3 large model for heavy async tasks.
- Models produce evidence; a versioned, deterministic **policy engine** makes pass/nudge/hold/block decisions from evidence + conversation policy + user preferences + tension state.
- Prompts and golden eval sets live in-repo; CI runs evals on prompt/model changes with per-language thresholds.
decisions.status_text: Accepted · 2026-10-18

decisions.title: Open-weight inference providers with zero data retention first; self-host trigger
decisions.summary:
Model aliases (initial):

| Alias | Primary | Alternate | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| guard (tier 1) | Qwen3Guard-Gen-0.6B (hot path), 4B (escalation/sampling) | Nemotron Safety Guard 8B v3; Llama Guard 4 for images; gpt-oss-safeguard-20b for policy-at-inference experiments | Apache 2.0; tri-clas…
decisions.text:
**Model aliases (initial):**

| Alias | Primary | Alternate | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `guard` (tier 1) | Qwen3Guard-Gen-0.6B (hot path), 4B (escalation/sampling) | Nemotron Safety Guard 8B v3; Llama Guard 4 for images; gpt-oss-safeguard-20b for policy-at-inference experiments | Apache 2.0; tri-class output maps to pass / nudge / hold |
| `mid` (tier 2) | Gemma 4 26B-A4B | Qwen3.5/3.6-35B-A3B; Qwen3.5-9B for cost | Pick default after a Hebrew/Arabic rephrase eval |
| `translate` | `mid` prompted for translation | Hy-MT2 7B/30B-A3B or TranslateGemma-12B per language pair only if an A/B shows gain and license permits | Stream to recipients |
| `large` (tier 3) | gpt-oss-120b (assistant/tool use), DeepSeek V4 Flash / V4.1 Flash (multilingual summaries) | Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, GLM-5.3-Flash, Mistral Large 3 (EU) | Avoid Kimi K3, Qwen3.8 flagship, Muse Spark Open (licenses/prices), Llama 4 (EU multimodal clause) |
| `stt` | Whisper large-v3-turbo | Qwen3-ASR 1.7B, Voxtral Mini Realtime after Hebrew/Arabic WER check | |
| `embed` | Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B | bge-m3 | CPU/shared L4 |

**Providers at launch (all OpenAI-compatible, behind the gateway):**
1. Fireworks AI (ZDR by default on open models; `store=false`; region-restricted deployments for EU when needed).
2. Groq (no retention by default + ZDR toggle; fastest decode; gpt-oss-120b and hosted guard backstop).
3. OVHcloud AI Endpoints (documented ZDR, EU-hosted, SOC 2 Type II/ISO 27001; hosted Qwen3Guard beta) with Scaleway as the EU alternate; Nebius once ZDR is confirmed in writing.
4. OpenRouter in ZDR-enforced mode as long-tail fallback only.
Together (ZDR opt-in), DeepInfra and Novita (no formal ZDR) are price benchmarks and may serve non-content workloads only. Lambda Inference API (winding down) and Helicone (maintenance mode) are excluded.

**Self-hosting:**
- **Tier 1 guard: self-host from private beta** (2× L4/L40S in the primary region, vLLM; ~$650–1,600/month) for latency, privacy and lack of hosted Qwen3Guard. Alpha may use OVH's hosted Qwen3Guard beta plus Groq backstop.
- **Tier 2: self-host when one alias sustains ~30–40M calls/month (~1–1.3M/day) or its API bill exceeds ~$3–5k/month for three consecutive months**; start with 2× H100 (redundancy) behind vLLM Router/llm-d; expect ~45–50% utilization as the real break-even.
- **Tier 3: stay on APIs** until well past 50–100M calls/month.
- **Confidential path:** pilot an attested provider (Privatemode, EU) for the most sensitive tier-3 tasks; own TEE GPU fleet only after product-market fit with an audit budget (sealing phase C, ADR-0003).

**Gateway:** `packages/ai-gateway` owns task-level routing and policy; beneath it, direct OpenAI-compatible adapters at first, with an OSS gateway (Bifrost or LiteLLM's Rust gateway) added when key management, budgets and fallbacks across many upstreams justify it.
decisions.status_text: Accepted · 2026-10-18 · Review quarterly (prices and models move monthly)

decisions.title: Mediator-gated release of message keys (fail-open vs fail-closed conversations)
decisions.summary: Each message is encrypted with a fresh key m.
decisions.text: Each message is encrypted with a fresh key `m`. The client wraps `m` to the Mediator key (always, unless level Off) and, only in fail-open conversations (Gentle/Standard, no hold/block scope rules, no minors), also under the conversation key `K_e`. Recipients get the `K_e` wrap only when the dispatcher releases it on a signed Mediator pass or, in fail-open conversations, on the sender's signed release or on an automatic release where a market's policy chose one (ADR-0023); never silently by default. In fail-closed conversations (Strict, Relay, hold/block scope, minors present) the client sends no `K_e` wrap; the Mediator creates it on pass or emits a conveyance instead. Relay/session originals are encrypted to the sender's devices and the Mediator only.
decisions.status_text: Accepted · 2026-10-18 · fail modes amended by ADR-0023 (L436, 2026-10-24; applied by wave 50 H, 2026-10-25)

decisions.title: Device streams with ephemeral ordered consumers and client-held cursors (amends ADR-0005)
decisions.summary: 1. Each live gateway connection reads its device's subject dev.<deviceId> through an ephemeral ordered consumer created at handshake and dropped at disconnect.
decisions.text:
1. Each live gateway connection reads its device's subject `dev.<deviceId>` through an **ephemeral ordered consumer** created at handshake and dropped at disconnect.
2. The **client holds its cursor** (`dseq`, cumulative acknowledgement) and sends it on resume; the gateway starts the consumer at `dseq + 1`. `dseq` is the stream sequence of the device subject.
3. When NATS has lost data (the requested start is before the stream's first sequence), the gateway starts from a **time-based** sequence so `dseq` never regresses, and tells the client `resync_required`; the client refetches by conversation `seq` from Postgres (the system of record).
4. There is **no connection registry**. Any gateway can serve any device; presence, typing, rate limits, handshake nonces and token revocations stay in Redis.
5. Durable consumers remain where they belong: the Mediator request queue (`MEDIATION_REQ`, consumer `mediator`), Mediator results (`MEDIATION_RES`, consumer `dispatcher`) and worker queues (`WQ_*`).
decisions.status_text: Accepted (lead, 2026-10-19) · 2026-10-19 (drafted by workstream H in doc-conformance audit #1, deviation C1-03; implements lead decision L50) · **Amends:** ADR-0005 ("every device has a durable consumer on its stream"; "Redis retained for … the connection registry")

decisions.title: Partition management in plain SQL; receipts as watermark rows (amends ADR-0004)
decisions.summary: 1. messages is PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at) with monthly sub-parents, each PARTITION BY HASH (conv_id) into N leaves (16 at launch, read from lucid_partition_config when a month is created).
decisions.text:
1. `messages` is `PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at)` with monthly sub-parents, each `PARTITION BY HASH (conv_id)` into N leaves (16 at launch, read from `lucid_partition_config` when a month is created). `overlays` uses the same scheme on its **own** `created_at`.
2. Partition DDL lives in two SQL functions created by migration 0001, `lucid_ensure_partitions(table, from, months)` and `lucid_drop_partitions_before(table, cutoff)`, shared by the migration and the worker job (`runPartitionMaintenance`, hourly, advisory lock, `PARTITION_MONTHS_AHEAD` = 3). No extension.
3. `receipts` is an unpartitioned watermark table keyed by `(conv_id, user_id)`; large groups add `receipt_counters`.
4. `(conv_id, seq)` uniqueness comes from the single sequencer (`UPDATE conversations SET last_seq = last_seq + 1 … RETURNING`); `(sender_device, client_key)` idempotency and global `msg_id` uniqueness live in the unpartitioned `message_idempotency` table, because partitioned unique indexes must include the partition keys.
5. Until the outbox-driven inbox updater (P2-C-04) exists, `inbox_summary` is updated in the send transaction (L40).
decisions.status_text: Accepted (lead, 2026-10-19) · 2026-10-19 (drafted by workstream H in doc-conformance audit #1, deviation C1-07; implements lead decisions L37 and L40) · **Amends:** ADR-0004 decision paragraph ("partitioning by `hash(conversation_id) × month` for `messages`, `overlays` and `receipts`; `pg_partman` for partition management")

decisions.title: Phase A Mediator key custody — KMS-wrapped key groups, unwrapped once into the Mediator's key adapter (amends ADR-0003 §3A)
decisions.summary: 1. At rest: each Mediator key group (mk_g<group>_v<version>: Ed25519 signing + X25519 agreement) is stored only as a blob encrypted under a KMS key-encryption key (stage 0: @lucid/kms-stub, AES-256-GCM under a master key; stage 1+: cloud KMS or OpenBao Transit KEK) whose Decrypt permission is gra…
decisions.text:
1. **At rest:** each Mediator key group (`mk_g<group>_v<version>`: Ed25519 signing + X25519 agreement) is stored only as a blob encrypted under a KMS key-encryption key (stage 0: `@lucid/kms-stub`, AES-256-GCM under a master key; stage 1+: cloud KMS or OpenBao Transit KEK) whose `Decrypt` permission is granted only to the Mediator service identity, every use audited.
2. **At startup:** the Mediator's KMS adapter performs one `Decrypt` per key group, holds the private bytes in a closure inside the adapter, zeroizes the KEK material, and exposes frozen handles with operations only. Startup fails (no readiness) if any key group cannot be loaded or the audit sink is down.
3. **Per message:** operations run in memory through `MediatorKeyOps`; `@lucid/mediation` and `@lucid/core` accept operation objects and never receive key bytes (P0-A-06-F2, P0-D-01-F9). No per-message KMS call.
4. **Never:** persisted plaintext keys, swap or core dumps on Mediator hosts, key bytes in logs, errors, metrics, heap snapshots of other roles, or any API returning private material.
5. **Rotation:** a new version per deployment or on schedule; new epochs wrap to it; older versions stay decrypt-only until their epochs expire (`docs/runbooks/key-rotation.md`).
6. **Phase B** replaces step 1's IAM gate with attestation-gated release (KMS releases the KEK only to measured confidential-VM images); steps 2–5 are unchanged.
decisions.status_text: Accepted (lead, 2026-10-19) · **Amended by:** ADR-0018 (decision 1: the stage-1 key-encryption key may be a secret-store master key per domain, envelope adapter `@lucid/kms-envelope`; accepted by the lead L184, pending owner) · 2026-10-19 (drafted by workstream H in doc-conformance audit #1, deviation C1-22; records lead decisions L36, L53, L54) · **Amends:** ADR-0003 decision 3 phase A ("KMS/HSM-held non-exportable keys") and `docs/05` §3.4 ("private keys are generated inside KMS/HSM … and are non-exportable")

decisions.text:
**(b).** `P` is shared per conversation under a labelled subkey of the current epoch key:

```
K_pk       = BLAKE2b-256(key = K_e, TBS(epoch-subkey, conv_id, u32be(epoch), "profile-key"))
sealed_key = nonce ‖ XChaCha20-Poly1305(K_pk, nonce, P, TBS(profile-key-share-aad, conv_id, u32be(epoch), user_id, u32be(key_version), key_commitment))
```

- A `ProfileKeyShare{user_id, key_version, key_commitment, sealed_key, writer_device_id}` is **self-authenticating**: readers accept `P` only when its commitment equals the `key_commitment` that the owner's rostered device signed in the `EncryptedProfile` (`acceptProfileKey`). Shares need no signature, and a member or the server can at most drop or replay one (readers keep the highest verified `key_version`).
- **Owner path:** a member's device posts its share for the conversation's current epoch when it first takes part (sends, or accepts the conversation) and after every change of `P`. It travels as a conversation log entry (`ConversationUpdate.profile_key`, field 10), so members get it live and on resume.
- **Rotation path:** the device that creates a new epoch re-shares, inside the new `EpochKeyBundle.profile_keys` (field 8, not covered by the bundle signature), every member's current `P` it holds. New members and new devices therefore read names from the bundle they open anyway, without any owner being online.
- **Revocation:** blocking someone (or a device leaving the owner's roster) creates `P'` with `key_version + 1`, a new `EncryptedProfile`, and new shares in every conversation except the 1:1 with the blocked user. Groups that contain the blocked user still receive `P'` (they are group members; leaving the group is the user's choice). Unblocking shares the current `P` in the 1:1 again. Member removal already rotates the epoch, so a removed member cannot read later shares; it keeps the old `P` until the owner's next rotation.
- The Mediator holds `K_e` (unless level Off) and already has `P` through `EncryptedProfile.wrap_m`; nothing new is disclosed to it.
decisions.status_text: Accepted (lead, 2026-10-19; renumbered from 0011 to avoid a clash with the device-streams ADR). Policy choice accepted: after a block, the rotated profile key is still shared in groups the blocked person belongs to (group membership already implies visibility of the profile).

decisions.title: Development backing services on Railway instead of local Docker
decisions.summary: 1. Backing services for development run on Railway (project lucid.chat, environment dev, EU region) as stock images with volumes: Postgres (Railway template), Redis (template), NATS 2.10.29 with JetStream and token auth, MinIO (pgsty/minio, the Compose build).
decisions.text:
1. Backing services for development run on **Railway** (project `lucid.chat`, environment `dev`, EU region) as stock images with volumes: Postgres (Railway template), Redis (template), NATS `2.10.29` with JetStream and token auth, MinIO (`pgsty/minio`, the Compose build). Reached from the development machine through Railway TCP proxies (Postgres over TLS; NATS token and Redis password over the proxy) and an HTTPS edge domain for S3.
2. The connection strings and dev-only secrets live in the **shared root `.env`** (git-ignored). `scripts/with-env.mjs` loads it for `pnpm env:doctor | dev:server | dev:mocks | db:migrate | test:integration` from the main checkout and from every agent worktree (resolved via the common git dir).
3. Integration tests get an **external-services mode** (`LUCID_TEST_SERVICES=external`, the default in `.env` and in CI): URLs from the environment, one `t_*` database per test file, no containers. Testcontainers remains the fallback when the variable is unset; tests that need to kill containers (`nats-loss`) run only in that mode.
4. `NATS_TOKEN` (or `nats://<token>@host`) is accepted by the server for token-authenticated NATS; staging+ keeps the credentials-file/mTLS plan (P1-H-06-F7).
5. Mocks (inference, SMS, push) stay local processes (`pnpm dev:mocks`).
6. `infra/compose` remains the reference service graph for CI, k6 and chaos drills; it is not started on the development machine during agent waves. Docker Desktop, if present, is capped at 4 GB RAM / 20 GB disk.
7. Operating limits for agent waves: at most three agents at once and three concurrent integration suites; worktree `node_modules` are removed at merge.

decisions.title: Device linking by QR with a device-to-device secret; key backups that carry the device identity
decisions.summary: 1. The new device shows the QR code (LinkOffer): its public keys, a server rendezvous id (link_id = the link challenge id), expiry, and a 32-byte link_secret that never leaves the two devices.
decisions.text:
1. **The new device shows the QR code** (`LinkOffer`): its public keys, a server rendezvous id (`link_id` = the link challenge id), expiry, and a 32-byte `link_secret` that never leaves the two devices. The primary learns the new device's keys over the optical channel, so the server cannot substitute them (the primary also compares the keys the server echoes). The primary answers with a `LinkApproval` signed by its device key **and** MACed with `link_secret` (keyed BLAKE2b), binding the offer digest, the server-assigned device id, the next roster version (signed by the primary, listing the new device as LINKED with exactly the offer's keys) and the digests of every hand-off part. The new device accepts only an approval with a valid MAC (so it comes from whoever scanned its own QR code), a roster self-signed by its PRIMARY that lists it with its own keys, and a valid approval signature by that primary. The server additionally verifies the approval signature with the primary's registered key and that the roster chains, and activates the device only after a claim signed with the new device's key.
2. **History keys travel as self-authenticating grants** (`EpochKeyGrant`, `ProfileKeyGrant`, `MessageKeyGrant`) in a hand-off sealed to the new device's X25519 key (fresh key per part, AAD bound to link, user, device and part). The receiver accepts a grant only against a record it verified: K_e against the signed bundle's commitment, P against the owner's signed profile, m by opening the envelope's AEAD. A forged hand-off can therefore only fail or be dropped. Linking does not rotate epochs (the new device gets the current K_e); revoking a device does (`device_unlinked`) and also rotates the profile key.
3. **A key backup (`BackupPayload` inside the existing `LUCIDBK1` blob) carries, by default, the backing-up device's identity** (Ed25519 seed and X25519 secret), the user's roster history and pinned peer rosters, and the same grants. On restore, if the backed-up device is still the roster's PRIMARY, the restored device signs a **handover** with the backed-up key (the next chained version names the new device PRIMARY and drops the old one): peers and the Mediator see an authorized update, not a reset, and the restored device rotates every conversation. A backup from a LINKED device, or without identity, restores history keys only; the roster then needs a QR link from the primary or a reset. Users can choose a backup without identity (`backupPayload({identity: undefined})`). The passphrase KDF stays Argon2id from the crypto runtime (ADR-0010) with the parameters in the header; the server stores the blob opaquely per user (`PUT/GET/DELETE /v1/me/backup`) and checks only its header.

decisions.title: Server KMS adapter: envelope encryption under a secret-store master key now, cloud KMS / OpenBao adapters later behind the same interfaces
decisions.summary: 1. Adapter now: envelope (option A), package @lucid/kms-envelope, selected with KMS_ADAPTER=envelope (the server port; the Mediator follows unless MEDIATOR_KMS_PROVIDER says otherwise).
decisions.text:
1. **Adapter now: envelope (option A)**, package `@lucid/kms-envelope`, selected with `KMS_ADAPTER=envelope` (the server port; the Mediator follows unless `MEDIATOR_KMS_PROVIDER` says otherwise). It is a new package, not a rename of `@lucid/kms-stub`, because the stub's name, refusals (`staging`, `production`) and README describe a stage-0 tool, and the envelope adapter is the one production accepts; the stub keeps its file format and now shares its operations core (`ops.ts`: the frozen sign / open-sealed handles, zeroizing `close()`, the fail-closed audit) with the envelope adapter, so the non-export guarantees exist once.
2. **Two domains, two master keys.** `server` (the KMS port's keys, table `server_kms_keys`, master key `LUCID_KMS_MASTER_KEY[_FILE]`, given to every role but the Mediator) and `mediator` (key groups, table `mediator_key_groups`, `LUCID_KMS_MEDIATOR_MASTER_KEY[_FILE]`, given to the Mediator only). The domain is in the envelope header and in the KEK derivation, so even the same master key could not open the other domain's rows. Production refuses the Mediator key in any process that runs more than the Mediator role, and the server key in a Mediator-only process.
3. **Envelope format v1** (`lucid-kms-envelope/v1`): magic `LKEV`, format version, algorithm (AES-256-GCM), domain, generation (u32), master key id (8 bytes of an HMAC of the master key), key id; the whole header is the AEAD's additional data. A blob cannot move to another key id, generation or domain; a header byte changed fails authentication. Spec and vector: `docs/mechanisms/mediator-keys.md` §Data, `packages/kms-envelope/test/format.test.ts`.
4. **Master key sources.** Read once at start, from a file of mode 0600 or stricter (preferred: a platform secret file) or a secret-store variable; the variable is removed from `process.env` right after. Production also refuses a key file inside a git working tree and a variable whose value a `.env*` file around the working directory (or `LUCID_ENV_FILE`) also holds: a developer `.env` is never a deployed process's secret store. Trade-off of the variable form, accepted and documented: the initial environment of a Linux process stays readable in `/proc/<pid>/environ` to the same user and root for the process lifetime; the file form leaves nothing there. *Amended by ADR-0019 (wave 23 A): production refuses the variable form altogether (`LUCID_KMS_KEK=env`); it accepts the file form and `transit` (the master key wrapped under a Transit KEK, never in the secret store).*
5. **Startup only.** Each process reads its domain's rows once, unwraps them, destroys the master key and keeps the key ring (server) or the operations-only `KeyService` (Mediator) in memory, as ADR-0013 decided. No per-message KMS call. A missing key, a wrong master key, a tampered or moved row, or an audit sink that throws fails the start.
6. **Generation and rotation.** Production never generates at start (`KMS_ENVELOPE_AUTOCREATE` is refused there); `pnpm --filter @lucid/server kms generate` creates keys. Key rotation = a new generation under the same master key (`generate --domain mediator --group <n>`; `generate --domain server --alias <a> --staged` then `promote` after every role restarted). Master-key rotation = a re-wrap job (`kms rewrap --domain …` with the new key as current and the old as `*_PREVIOUS_*`; processes accept both during the window). One-way imports from the `local` key file and the stub directory keep existing data readable and the dispatcher's pins valid.
7. **Audit.** Every key operation goes through the existing `AuditHook` (content-free `{ ts, op, key_id, outcome, error_code, role }`, fail-closed). The server sends them to the content-free log as `kms.op` (lifecycle at info, per-use operations at debug, refusals as warnings with their `E_KMS_*` code); the CLI writes them as JSON lines on stderr. A durable append-only audit sink is follow-up P1-A-05-F1.
8. **Later adapters** (options B and C) implement the same two interfaces (`Kms` for the server port, `KeyService` for the Mediator) and read the same rows: only the unwrap of the KEK changes (a Transit or cloud `Decrypt` instead of the local HKDF), so the switch is a configuration change plus a one-time re-wrap, not a new code path.
decisions.status_text: Accepted (lead, L184; pending owner) — proposed by workstream A with D's key design, wave 19, 2026-10-21 (lead decision L179 asked for it); accepted with two master keys (server, Mediator); the HSM half of P1-A-05 stays open · **Amended by:** ADR-0019 (wave 23 A: the KEK the process never holds — OpenBao Transit wraps each domain's master key; decision 4's variable form is no longer accepted in production); **ADR-0022 §12 (L437, lead L439, 2026-10-24): decision 4 (the variable form) is accepted on a Railway-hosted stage in the sealed-and-consumed form** — a Railway sealed service variable that the start command writes into a 0600 tmpfs file and removes from the environment before `exec` (`LUCID_KMS_KEK_SOURCE=railway_sealed`), so the `/proc/<pid>/environ` trade-off of decision 4 does not apply; the raw variable form stays refused in production · **Amends:** ADR-0013 decision 1 (the stage-1 key-encryption key may be a secret-store master key, not only a cloud KMS or OpenBao Transit key) · **Related:** ADR-0013, `docs/05-security-privacy.md` §3.4, `docs/mechanisms/mediator-keys.md`, `docs/runbooks/secrets.md` §Envelope KMS, `docs/runbooks/deploy.md` §2 and §8.2, checklist P1-A-05, P2-H-08-F27-F1, P2-H-08-F27-F2

decisions.title: A key-encryption key the process never holds: OpenBao Transit first, a cloud KMS as the same shape later
decisions.summary: 1. First KEK adapter: OpenBao Transit (open source, Vault-API-compatible, self-hosted on the VM or beside it; brew install openbao for development).
decisions.text:
1. **First KEK adapter: OpenBao Transit** (open source, Vault-API-compatible, self-hosted on the VM or beside it; `brew install openbao` for development). One named Transit key per domain, `lucid-server` and `lucid-mediator`, created with `exportable=false` and `allow_plaintext_backup=false`: the KEK exists only inside OpenBao. A cloud KMS adapter (AWS KMS, GCP Cloud KMS, Scaleway Key Manager) is **the same shape later**: the same two calls (wrap, unwrap), the same row, a different client.
2. **What changes: only where the per-domain master key comes from.** With `LUCID_KMS_KEK=transit` the 32-byte master key of a domain is not in the secret store. It rests in the new table `kms_master_keys` (migration `0032_wave23_kms_master_keys`) as Transit's own ciphertext (`vault:v<n>:…`) under the domain's Transit key, and the process asks Transit to `decrypt` it **once at start** (one audited `kek_unwrap`). From there everything is ADR-0018 unchanged: the same envelope rows (`server_kms_keys`, `mediator_key_groups`), the same `master_key_id` in every header, the same generations, states, `kms_audit`, `KeyService` and `Kms` interfaces, the same key ring and operations core. No per-message call. `LUCID_KMS_KEK=file` keeps the ADR-0018 behaviour byte for byte.
3. **Identity binds the KEK to a role.** Each process authenticates to Transit with its own identity (a 0600 token file, or an AppRole whose secret id is a 0600 file); OpenBao's policy allows the server identity `update` on `transit/decrypt/lucid-server` only and the Mediator identity `update` on `transit/decrypt/lucid-mediator` only; only the operator (the `kms` CLI) may `encrypt`; no identity may `create` keys through `encrypt`. The server configuration refuses the other domain's key name in a process (production), and the loader refuses a row wrapped under another key name than the one configured before any call. A Mediator token cannot unwrap the server master key and the reverse, even with the rows in hand.
4. **Migration and break-glass are one `kms rewrap`.** `kms rewrap --domain <d> --to transit` generates a fresh master key in the CLI's memory, wraps it through Transit (`kek_wrap`), installs the `kms_master_keys` row and re-wraps every row of the domain under it **in one transaction** (a domain never has rows under a KEK-wrapped master without the row that holds it, or the other way round); the plaintext is zeroized, never written. Running it again rotates the master key under Transit (the earlier row is kept `retired_at`). `kms rewrap --domain <d> --to file` is the way back: the operator generates a new secret-store key, the rows go back under it and the Transit row is retired. Both need Transit to answer once; a lost OpenBao (no backup, no unseal) loses the keys exactly as a lost master key did.
5. **Fail closed, content-free.** A bounded timeout per attempt; retries only on transport failures, 5xx and 429, never on a refusal (an expired or wrong token, a policy that does not allow the key: `E_KMS_KEK_DENIED`); unreachable after the retries: `E_KMS_KEK_UNAVAILABLE`; a wrong key name or a ciphertext of another key: `E_KMS_UNWRAP_FAILED`; the unwrapped bytes must reproduce the row's `master_key_id`. Every KEK call goes through the existing fail-closed audit hook as `kek_unwrap` / `kek_wrap` with the master key's public fingerprint, never the key or the ciphertext, into `kms.op` and `kms_audit`, and is counted in `lucid_kms_ops_total{op,outcome}`. Errors carry the HTTP status and a static message, never a response body, token or key. Production requires `https://` (an optional private CA bundle and / or an SPKI pin), and a token **file** or AppRole, never a token variable.
6. **Production no longer accepts a master key in a variable** (`LUCID_KMS_KEK=env` and every `LUCID_KMS_*MASTER_KEY` variable are refused with `NODE_ENV=production`; the file form and `transit` are accepted). ADR-0018 accepted the variable form with a documented trade-off (`/proc/<pid>/environ`); with a KEK available the trade-off is no longer worth carrying. Railway (variables only) can therefore run the envelope adapter in production mode only with `transit`, which matches L179: Railway holds test data; the alpha environment is a VM with secret files and OpenBao.
decisions.status_text: Accepted (lead, L229; status line corrected L434, 2026-10-24) · amended by ADR-0022· **Amended by:** ADR-0022 (DC-1, 2026-10-24, accepted by the lead L432: the OpenBao seal — Shamir 2 of 3 with shares on two keyholders' phones under biometric-gated hardware keys plus one offline SLIP-39 share, `init -pgp-keys`, an unseal agent and a ceremony the phones perform; a cloud-KMS auto-unseal later keeps the same holders as recovery keys); **amended by ADR-0022 §12 (L437, lead L439, 2026-10-24): decision 6 relaxed to the Railway-sealed, start-command-consumed form on a Railway-hosted stage; the OpenBao seal is optional hardening (step 1), auto-unsealed by the static seal; the Keyholder shares become the disaster-recovery root of an escrowed recovery key, never the restart path** · **Amends:** ADR-0018 (§What stays open, first bullet; decision 4: production no longer accepts a master key in a variable) · **Related:** ADR-0013, `docs/05-security-privacy.md` §3.4, `docs/mechanisms/mediator-keys.md` §KEK sources, `docs/runbooks/secrets.md` §OpenBao Transit, `docs/runbooks/deploy.md` §2.1, `docs/runbooks/key-rotation.md` §4.2, `docs/07-external-services.md` (Secrets/KMS row), checklist P1-A-05-F2

decisions.title: Current, best-supported technology: dependency currency policy, and TypeScript 7 timing
decisions.summary: 1. Rule (every dependency).
decisions.text:
1. **Rule (every dependency).** Lucid runs each dependency on a **current, actively maintained major that the packages we depend on support well**: state of the art, well understood, stable, not experimental. Nothing deprecated, end-of-life or unmaintained is added or kept. A newer major that is faster or better but breaks widely used packages we rely on (lint, tests, Expo / React Native, build, database tooling) is **not** adopted early; the blocker and a dated re-check trigger are recorded, and we move when the ecosystem has caught up. Longevity and performance are balanced against stability and third-party support, with support the tie-breaker.
2. **Evidence before a bump.** Package metadata (`npm view <pkg> version deprecated`, peer ranges), the release notes, the project's issue tracker for the new major, and community experience (GitHub issues, Reddit, maintainers' write-ups). A bump is a wave with the suites it reaches (rule 15), never a lockfile-only change.
3. **The board.** `docs/runbooks/dependency-currency.md` (A 46) lists every direct dependency with its pinned version, the current stable major, deprecation status, the blocker if we are behind, and the re-check date. `pnpm deps:check` fails CI on a deprecated direct dependency and on an exception row whose re-check date has passed. A owns it; every wave that touches a `package.json` updates its rows.
4. **TypeScript: 6.0.3 now, 7.x on three conditions.** We stay on 6.0.3 (the 7.0 language, the stable toolchain). We adopt 7.x in the first month in which all three hold: (a) typescript-eslint has a **stable** release that supports the installed 7.x; (b) Expo's current SDK documents TypeScript 7 support and the config-loading issue is closed; (c) the declaration-emit regressions listed above are closed in a shipped 7.x patch. Until then A records a monthly readiness probe: `tsgo --noEmit` (from `@typescript/native-preview`, run ad hoc, not added as a dependency) over every workspace tsconfig, comparing error parity and wall time with `tsc`, so the gain is measured, not assumed. The 5.x line is not returned to.
5. **Not chosen.** (i) 7 for `tsc` with 6 aliased for lint: two compilers, two sets of diagnostics, no linting of what we ship, for a type-check that is already fast at our size. (ii) Dropping type-aware lint to allow 7 now: the content-leak and adapters-only rules in `packages/eslint-plugin-lucid` need the type checker. (iii) ts7-eslint: unmaintained-by-the-project code in the security-relevant lint path.
decisions.status_text: Accepted (owner L390, 2026-10-23; lead) · **Related:** `docs/09-decision-log.md` L386 (TypeScript 6.0.3), L390; `docs/runbooks/typescript-6-move.md`; `docs/runbooks/dependency-currency.md` (A 46, the living board); CLAUDE.md "Current, best-supported technology"; `docs/briefs/_common.md` rule 16; open decision 0eb

decisions.status_text: Accepted (lead, L493, 2026-10-27; written in ARCH-3, Opus 5.5) · **Amends:** ADR-0006 (model tiering: the tiers become the stages of a cascade per task) · **Related:** ADR-0007 (providers, self-host trigger), ADR-0009 (Mediator-gated release: a client's verdict never releases), ADR-0021 (device-held context, excerpts), ADR-0023 (fail-safe behaviour: the ask window, "Still checking", tier 0 guards the ask), ADR-0025 (party-private mediation, MED-2, written at the same time: the cascade's mediation stage), `docs/11-ai-architecture.md` §4, `docs/mechanisms/mediation-pipeline.md` §Guard categories and the second opinion · **Owner's words (L492 (1), 2026-10-27):** "Use the fast and less capable models to answer quickly and do things within their ability, and move to stronger models if there's ambiguity, or in tasks and cases where a stronger model would be far better — for both cost and response time." On-device models, "notably if they have low false negatives", serve as quick triage and pass on to stronger models. "We get more false positives with weaker models, so when there's a positive we likely want to pass it into stronger judgement." · **Research:** `docs/01-research/inference-cascades-2026-10.md` · **Rows:** L492-F1 (this ADR), L492-F5 (the cascade simulation in every eval run, wave 60 D), L492-F7 (the build in the registry and router), L492-F8 (the on-device tier), L492-F9 … F15 (§13)

cards.group: Decide — architecture questions with down-the-line implications
cards.title: When Lucid is slow: may a sender send their own message unchecked?
cards.context: Measured: in region about 1 message in 100 waits more than 1.5 seconds for its check; during a provider outage, all of them do. Today such a message goes out unchecked, the rule you rejected. The new design holds it and shows 'Still checking' with two buttons: keep waiting, or send now unchecked. The offer appears only in a 1:1 with a known contact, never with a minor, never in Strict, Relay or scope-ruled chats, only when the fast local check is clean and the reader allows it, at most 30 times an hour; the message is always marked 'Not checked' and a late block still applies. Saying no means a provider outage is a messaging outage for everyone.

cards.group: Decide — architecture questions with down-the-line implications
cards.title: During a long outage, may contacts' chats resume automatically?
cards.context: If the check stays unavailable for a long time, Gentle and Standard chats between contacts could resume by themselves after a long, marked wait (30–60 seconds), or only when a person taps 'send now'. Automatic resumption is the smallest thing that is still a give-up-and-send, so the design keeps it as a market setting that starts off everywhere.
cards.recommendation: Keep the option, start off; revisit after the first measured outage.
